description: We are computer science master's students. We are interested in building solutions that solve real problems. Our interests include machine learning, cybersecurity, software engineering, systems and AI.
summary:
Earth System Trend Detective is a web tool that shows what is changing on Earth, where, how fast, and whether the change is statistically real. We started with 156 collections in NASA's Earthdata catalogue across four data centres (GES DISC, NSIDC, LP DAAC and PO.DAAC), narrowing them to 43 products covering 2005–2024. These contained 2,212 variables. After removing quality flags, error estimates and duplicates, 201 remained; 178 were downloadable for every month.

Each variable became 240 monthly maps on a 5-degree global grid. We tested trends in every grid cell, then selected 20 variables to display: 6 headline variables, like air temperature and sea level, and 14 data-selected variables that best represent where and how strongly the Earth system is changing.

A 3D globe shows each variable's change per decade. Clicking a tile, region or hotspot reveals its 20-year monthly time series, rate of change with a confidence interval, p-value and plain-language verdict. This addresses all four parts of the challenge: selecting variables, exploring data for any location, showing its monthly time series, and testing and explaining its trend. Because trends vary by place and are easy to overstate, the tool shows which changes the data support.
details:
Github repo link: https://github.com/swetha-ew2/nasa

WHAT IT DOES

For 20 Earth system variables, the tool shows what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is significant. A 3D globe is coloured by each variable's rate of change per decade. Bright tiles have a statistically significant trend and faded tiles do not. Users can click any 5-degree tile, one of 58 IPCC regions, a global result, or a hotspot (a group of neighbouring tiles that change in the same direction). They can also drag a box on the globe to test any area they chooseEach one opens a monthly time series with a 12-month average and a trend line, the rate with a 95% confidence interval, a p-value, an effect size and a one-sentence verdict. A short tour and a question flow (pick a theme, a question, then a place) help first time users find the right data. The 'Early signs' tab lists changes that just missed the strict test and could be potential new trends in the future.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data. We searched NASA Earthdata for monthly products that cover 2005-2024: MERRA-2, GLDAS, FLDAS, GPM IMERG, GPCP, MiCASA, MODIS, and PO.DAAC sea surface temperature and sea level. From 201 candidate variables we extracted 178, averaged each month onto a 5-degree grid (240 maps per variable) and checked every value range against its units.

2. Trends. In each grid cell we removed the seasonal cycle, then computed the Sen slope per decade (the median of all pairwise slopes) with a 95% interval, and a Mann-Kendall test with the variance inflated for month-to-month autocorrelation. We control the false discovery rate at 5% across cells and across regions, so a map of many cells does not produce false alarms.

3. Variable selection. Choosing from many variables is the first problem a trend detective meets, so we let the data decide. Each variable's trend map is turned into one vector. Starting from the 6 headline variables, forward selection (orthogonal matching pursuit) adds, one at a time, the variable that best reconstructs the trend maps of the whole pool, until 14 more are chosen. The 20 variables reconstruct about 65% of the pool's trend patterns. We repeated the selection on 20 bootstrap samples of the globe to see which picks are stable, and listed which near-duplicate variables each pick stands in for.

4. Regions and hotspots. The 58 IPCC AR6 reference regions are fixed in advance. Each 5-degree tile counts toward the region that contains its centre, regions with fewer than 3 tiles of data are not tested, and regions are corrected for multiple testing together. For each variable we grouped neighbouring significant tiles with the same sign, ranked the groups by area and effect size, and tested each group's average series. Because hotspots are picked for looking significant, the app labels them exploratory. Users can draw a custom box and the browser averages the tiles inside it and runs the same trend test, labelled exploratory because the area is chosen after looking at the map.

5. App. Results are precomputed into JSON, so the site is static and fast.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Students and members of the public can ask a question about a place or a variable and see whether the data support an answer. The app says plainly when a trend is not significant, shows the confidence interval next to the rate, and explains each test in simple words. We hope it teaches that a trend needs both a size and evidence.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

- We wanted the 20 variables on screen to show different things, so we chose them step by step. Each variable has a map of where and how strongly it is changing across the globe. We began with 6 headline variables. Then, one at a time, we added the variable that explained the most of the change patterns still missing from the set, measured against all 149 candidates. Together the 20 explain about 65% of the patterns in the whole pool. To test the result, we removed each variable in turn to see what was lost, and repeated the selection on 20 resampled versions of the globe to see which picks stay. Each variable on screen adds something the others do not already show.

- Opposite trends of one variable, for example precipitation rising in one region and falling in another, appear together as hotspots on the same globe.

- Non-significant results are kept and explained in "Early signs" because we found those interesting to show.

- The brief asks for one region's time series. We tested every 5-degree tile on the globe, about 290,000 series, so users can see where change is happening before they pick a place.

- Even if nothing were changing, a standard test marks about 1 tile in 20 as a trend by luck. On a map with thousands of tiles, that puts hundreds of false trends on screen. We added a correction, so only about 1 in 20 of the tiles we show as significant should be wrong.

- The 58 standard IPCC regions give a fair, fixed way to look anywhere on Earth, but a fixed list can miss local patterns. So for each variable the app also finds its own hotspots, groups of neighbouring tiles that change the same way, such as precipitation rising over the Southern Ocean and falling over the Eastern Pacific. We pick them because they look significant, so we label them leads to explore.

- Users can draw their own box on the globe and get a trend test computed in the browser on the spot.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, SciPy, netCDF4, h5netcdf, earthaccess, regionmask) for data access and statistics. React, TypeScript, Vite and MapLibre GL JS for the globe. NASA GIBS imagery for the globe background. Hosted on Vercel. No special hardware.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Twenty years is a short record, so trends can reflect natural variability such as El Nino. The autocorrelation correction is slightly liberal (about 6% false positives at a nominal 5% in our simulation). The 5-degree grid smooths small regions. Land models can disagree with each other, and we show that. These caveats are listed in the app.

USE OF SI

We used SI to help write the analysis code, the web app code and refine text. Ideation and all decisions are our own. All results come from NASA data processed by that code.
The demo submission made use of SI voice from elevenlabs to ensure everything was clear and easy to understand. Apart from this, the project contains no SI-generated images, audio or video, and no NASA logos or branding.
